page: UpCloud PREMIUM-8xCPU-64GB is a Premium family virtual server built on the KVM hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an AMD EPYC 9575F processor operating at 2.0 GHz. The configuration includes 8 vCPUs mapped to 8 physical cores with a single thread per core, utilizing a shared CPU allocation model. The system is equipped with 64.0 GB of system memory, providing a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio with 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage consists of a bundled 300 GB SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU accelerators are present on this instance.

Benchmark data reveals highly capable single-core performance alongside moderate multi-core and memory write capabilities. The server achieves top-tier status in single-core metrics, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance reaching 3567.67 and single-threaded gzip compression and bzip3 decompression scoring in the top 10%. However, multi-core performance and memory write speeds present clear tradeoffs. The stress-ng multi-core CPU performance and Geekbench multi-core scores fall within the average range. Notably, the PassMark memory score and large-block memory write bandwidth of 19.66 GB/sec are positioned in the bottom 25%, indicating potential bottlenecks during heavy, uncached memory write operations.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the PREMIUM-8xCPU-64GB offers a high memory density relative to its vCPU count, making it a viable option for memory-intensive workloads that do not require dedicated CPU pinning. The shared CPU allocation model reduces overall infrastructure costs but introduces potential resource contention compared to dedicated instances. Given its strong single-threaded execution and balanced database performance, this server is well-suited for relational database hosting, text processing, static web serving, and lightweight software compilation. It is less suitable for memory-write-heavy applications or medium-to-large language model inference due to weaker memory write bandwidth and lower LLM generation speeds.
